title: Excursion-Resolved Thermodynamic Inference without Observing Reverse Transitions
abstract: Experiments often detect only selected transitions, leaving the underlying state dynamics and dissipation hidden. We show that waiting-time distributions between directed visible events can reconstruct the boundary dynamics without observing the reverse of every detected transition. Under a simple source-target closure condition, they determine visible rates and the hidden excursions connecting observed states, yielding a rigorous lower bound on total entropy production that improves the standard waiting-time estimate when reverse events are available. Remarkably, observing only a spanning directed cycle is sufficient to identify the full Markov generator, even when all reverse cycle edges and other microscopic transitions remain unseen.
summary: This paper develops a method to estimate entropy production in Markovian systems when only a subset of transitions are observed. By analyzing waiting-time distributions across these visible events, the authors derive an excursion-resolved bound ($\sigma_{ERW}$) that is rigorously shown to be a tighter lower bound on the true entropy production than standard estimators. This advances the field by quantifying the information lost due to incomplete experimental observation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of reconstructing underlying state dynamics and quantifying entropy production when experimental measurements only capture a subset of possible transitions, leaving reverse processes unobserved.
main_result: It establishes a rigorous hierarchy of entropy production bounds ($\sigma \ge \sigma_{ERW} \ge \sigma_{WTD}$), showing that analyzing waiting-time distributions across observed transitions ($\sigma_{ERW}$) provides a tighter lower bound than standard methods ($\sigma_{WTD}$).
method: The core method involves analyzing joint next-label/time densities to reconstruct the boundary propagator and hidden-excursion kernel, allowing for the calculation of the excursion-resolved entropy production estimator ($\sigma_{ERW}$).
model_or_system: The analysis is based on an irreducible stationary continuous-time Markov jump process on a finite state space, modeled using microscopic rate matrices (generators $\mathbf{W}$).
key_observables:
Entropy production rates ($\sigma, \sigma_{ERW}, \sigma_{WTD}$), visible event rates ($
u_\ell$), and the hidden-excursion kernel $F(t)$.
important_parameters: The source–target closure condition ($U=V$) is crucial for the reconstruction; the analysis also uses kinetic scales ($b_{ij}$) and edge affinities ($a_{ij}$) in numerical examples.
main_assumptions: The primary assumptions include the source–target closure condition ($U=V$) and the assumption that the boundary-resolved trajectory follows a physical coarse trajectory.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the information hierarchy, comparing the true entropy production ($\sigma$) against the excursion-resolved bound ($\sigma_{ERW}$) and the standard waiting-time bound ($\sigma_{WTD}$), demonstrating how $\sigma_{ERW}$ captures information missed by $\sigma_{WTD}$.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework by defining the Markov process, deriving the various entropy estimators ($\sigma_{ERW}$ and $\sigma_{WTD}$), establishing the inequality hierarchy ($\sigma \ge \sigma_{ERW} \ge \sigma_{WTD}$), and concluding with numerical examples showing the recovery of full dynamics from partial observations.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful theoretical tool for analyzing non-equilibrium processes in mesoscopic physics, directly applicable to understanding energy dissipation in systems where measurement limitations obscure the full dynamical landscape.
